I have been farming these 10.1 mu for twenty years, and I know every piece of it. My family has six mouths, and some of them work off-farm, so I cannot spend all day in the fields. That is why wheat-maize is my backbone — it is mechanized, the income is stable, and I get two crops from the same land. I keep 2.1 mu of cotton because the price can be good, but I will not plant more than that because cotton is labor-intensive and I have to pick it myself when my children are away working.

Right now it is late April. My wheat is already in the ground and greening up. I sowed an improved variety like Jimai 22 last October — it performs well here in Quzhou. I will topdress nitrogen at jointing and irrigate three times total: once now to help the wheat recover from winter, once at booting, and once during grain filling. The wheat ground was prepared with rotary tillage before sowing, which is what we always do here. I will spray herbicide once and do one or two more sprays for aphids and rust if I see them.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I need to get maize in the ground fast — the window is only about ten days. I will plant a hybrid like Denghai 605 using no-tillage direct seeding into the wheat stubble. This saves me time, fuel, and labor, which matters because I am managing much of this alone. Summer maize needs less irrigation than wheat because the rains usually come in July and August, but I will irrigate twice if the weather turns dry — once at the big trumpet stage and once during grain filling. Two pesticide sprays should be enough: herbicide at sowing and insecticide for corn borer later.

For my 2.1 mu of cotton, I will deep plough first because cotton roots need loose, deep soil. I will plant a hybrid Bt cotton variety in late April. Cotton needs more fertilizer than grain crops to produce bolls, so I apply a bit more potash. I have well water, so I will irrigate twice during flowering and boll setting. Even with Bt cotton, I still need to spray several times for aphids, mites, and bollworm, so I plan about seven applications total. I expect around 550 jin per mu of seed cotton — not the highest, but reliable for the effort I can put in.

I do not chase the highest possible yield because that means risking too much money on extra inputs. With off-farm income in the family, I prefer a safe, middle path: good seeds, enough fertilizer to feed the crop, irrigation when the plants really need it, and keeping the pests under control without going overboard.
